title: Ensemble theory of thermodiffusion
authors: R. Belousov, J. Elliott, A. Erzberger
abstract: Heat flow sustained by a temperature difference generates a gradient of matter as observed, for example, in atomistic simulations of hard-core gases. We use path-ensemble theory to represent the coupled thermal and diffusive transport by dynamics on a graph. Calibrated from a single equilibrium simulation, this model accurately predicts nonequilibrium mass distribution in a hard-core gas across a wide range of applied temperature gradients. It also enables estimation of transport properties, such as the Soret coefficient, using analytical expressions.
summary: This paper develops an ensemble theory approach to model thermodiffusion in a hard-core gas under a temperature gradient. By using path-ensemble theory calibrated against equilibrium simulations, the authors successfully predict non-equilibrium mass and temperature profiles. The key finding is that incorporating detailed kinetic connectivity information (KC) into the graph structure is essential for accurately capturing coupled thermal and diffusive transport phenomena.
main_problem: The study of thermodiffusion, which describes the coupling between heat flow and matter transport (diffusion) in a system subjected to a temperature gradient.
main_result:
The path-ensemble theory accurately predicts non-equilibrium mass distribution profiles for a hard-core gas under $\Delta T 
eq 0$, yielding a simple formula for the Soret coefficient ($S_T$).
method: The authors employ path-ensemble theory, calibrating dynamics using microcanonical principles derived from equilibrium simulations to model non-equilibrium transport.
model_or_system: The system is a hard-core gas confined between two thermalizing walls. The dynamics are modeled on a lattice structure, governed by transition probabilities derived from maximizing the $\mu$-caliber subject to energy and matter conservation constraints.
key_observables: Mass distribution ($ho$), kinetic temperature ($T$), and the Soret coefficient ($S_T = D_T / D$).
important_parameters: Temperature gradient ($\Delta T$), lattice site energies ($\epsilon_i$), and time/space discretization parameters.
main_assumptions: The theory assumes all microscopic realizations of a path are equally probable, and it compares two graph connectivity schemes (Kinetic Connectivity vs. Nearest-Neighbor) to capture the necessary microscopic details.
figures_summary:
Figure 1 shows molecular dynamics results ($ho$ and $T$) exhibiting opposing gradients when $\Delta T 
eq 0$. Figure 3 compares MD simulations with predictions from the KC model (accurate) versus the NN scheme (fails) for non-equilibrium profiles.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical problem, develops the path-ensemble theory based on microcanonical principles, compares two graph connectivity schemes (KC vs. NN), and demonstrates that only the detailed Kinetic Connectivity approach correctly predicts the steady-state transport properties.
why_interesting: While focused on classical gas dynamics, the rigorous application of ensemble theory to non-equilibrium steady states—especially deriving macroscopic coefficients from microscopic path statistics—provides a powerful theoretical template applicable to open quantum systems far from equilibrium.
